title: Successful Nucleoside Analog and Corticosteroid Therapy for Chronic Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy in a Patient With Hepatitis B Virus Liver Cirrhosis
case_prompt:
A 44-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of progressive bilateral tingling and muscle weakness in his hands and feet. The paresthesias worsened until he became unable to move his extremities and was almost totally bedridden with irritating distal sensations. He denied any history of head or back trauma.

On examination, he was fully alert, with normal vital signs. He appeared slightly anemic and mildly icteric. Neurologic examination showed hyporeflexia in all four limbs, Medical Research Council muscle power grade 3/5 in the upper limbs and 1/5 in the lower limbs, and hypesthesia in all extremities without pathological reflexes.

Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL, platelets 116 000/mm3, aspartate aminotransferase 51 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 56 U/L, total bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL, prothrombin time 14.3 s (INR 1.3), albumin 2.6 g/dL, total protein 7.0 g/dL, creatinine 0.59 mg/dL, and normal electrolytes. Viral tests were positive for HBsAg and HBeAg, with an HBV DNA load of 1.65 × 105 IU/mL, and negative for HCV and HIV. Abdominal ultrasound showed minimal ascites.

Nerve conduction studies demonstrated prolongation of motor distal latency and F-wave latency and reduced motor conduction velocity in both sensory and motor nerves, consistent with axonal demyelination. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed 7 lymphocytes/mm3 and a protein concentration of 135 mg/dL. Serum protein electrophoresis revealed polyclonal gamma-globulinemia. Brain MRI identified a lacunar infarction. The patient declined biopsy.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy — “Our CIDP diagnosis was based on the clinical, electrodiagnostic, and CSF analysis criteria. Specifically, our patient had a chronic onset of progressive, symmetric, proximal-to-distal, and bilateral muscle weakness with sensory abnormalities persisting for more than 2 months, met 3 of the 4 electrodiagnostic criteria, and exhibited an increased CSF protein concentration.”  
2. Type I cryoglobulin-associated vasculitic neuropathy — “Serum protein electrophoresis and MRI were conducted to exclude other differential diagnoses, including type I cryoglobulin-associated vasculitic neuropathy, multifocal motor neuropathy, and the polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal gammopathy, and skin changes syndrome.”  
3. Multifocal motor neuropathy — “Serum protein electrophoresis and MRI were conducted to exclude other differential diagnoses, including type I cryoglobulin-associated vasculitic neuropathy, multifocal motor neuropathy, and the polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal gammopathy, and skin changes syndrome.”  
4. POEMS syndrome — “Serum protein electrophoresis and MRI were conducted to exclude other differential diagnoses, including type I cryoglobulin-associated vasculitic neuropathy, multifocal motor neuropathy, and the polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal gammopathy, and skin changes syndrome.”  
5. Type II or III mixed cryoglobulinemia — “However, type II or III mixed cryoglobulin was not excluded because the cryoglobulin and complement level examination could not be performed in our laboratory.”
